content.title: WHY YOUR {{HEALTHY}} MEAL PREP ISN'T ACTUALLY HEALTHY
facts: **Overcooking broccoli** – Boiling it for more than 5 minutes leaches out most of the vitamin C into the water; steam it for 3-4 minutes instead.
**Draining and rinsing canned beans** – Skipping this step means you're eating extra sodium; a quick rinse cuts it by roughly 40%.
**Adding oil to a cold pan** – Letting oil sit on high heat before food goes in breaks it down into harmful compounds; add oil right before the food.
**Salting vegetables before roasting** – This draws water out too early and leaves you with soggy, steamed veggies instead of crispy ones.
**Using the same board for raw meat and veggies** – Even after wiping it down, cross-contamination risk stays high; always use separate boards.
**Storing olive oil near the stove** – Heat and light break it down fast, turning a heart-healthy fat rancid within weeks.
**Microwaving in the takeout container** – Many plastic containers aren't microwave-safe and can leach chemicals into your food when heated.
**Tossing the cooking water from vegetables** – That water often holds a good chunk of the nutrients that leached out; save it for soups or sauces.
**Cutting garlic and using it immediately** – This skips the time it needs to activate its beneficial compounds; let it rest 10 minutes after chopping.

content.caption:
Let's talk about a few of these in more detail. Broccoli loses so much of its vitamin C in boiling water because the vitamin is heat-sensitive and water-soluble — it literally dissolves out into the liquid you're pouring down the drain. Garlic is a sneaky one too: the moment you crush or chop it, an enzyme reaction starts that creates allicin, its main beneficial compound, but that reaction needs a few minutes of air exposure to fully develop before heat destroys it. And that cooking water you're tossing? It's not just flavorless waste — it carries dissolved minerals and vitamins that leached out during boiling, so reusing it in a soup base means you're not losing those nutrients after all. Of course, everyone's kitchen habits are different, so start with the swap that feels easiest.
